---
title: Modeling what repeats, nests and unfolds
subtitle: Multilevel and advanced models
bibliography: references.bib
---








The last two parts ended the same way, and I said it out loud each time. In the linear models I treated every row as an independent observation and told you where that was true by design (one row per animal in the histology data) and where it would stop being true. In the generalized linear models I did it again, knowingly, in every chapter, and each time I wrote down what it cost and promised to come back:

- The wire attempts of one mouse were treated as interchangeable draws. Sixty-three mice completed about eight attempts each, and the intraclass correlation of the crossing times turned out to be about a third (@sec-linear-regression-assumptions).
- The yes or no of the hanging wire test was squeezed into one row per mouse, which avoids the dependence by throwing the repeated attempts away (@sec-logistic-regression).
- The 59 hippocampal neurons of the spike counts come from three patients, with well over a hundred trials each. A random intercept per neuron was previewed at the end and left as a preview (@sec-count-regression).
- Nine attempts per mouse made a plain binomial too sure of itself, and the open-field mice, tested on six days, were analyzed as if each day were a different mouse (@sec-beta-robust-regression).
- The cells we count in the histology arc sit in sections that sit in animals, and @sec-linear-models-reflection said plainly that "each row is an independent observation" is a bet, not a fact.

Later has arrived (@fig-multilevel-intro-hook pictures the problem: one mouse, seen again and again). This page is the doorway into the part where the structure we have been ignoring becomes the thing we model. It has three jobs: to show you, with data you already know, why rows from the same animal are not independent evidence; to introduce the one idea that repairs it, which is called partial pooling; and to be the map of the part, which you will find at the end. It fits no `brms` model: those belong to @sec-multilevel-varying-intercepts onward.

![The same mouse tested again and again is one mouse, not many.](images/multilevel-intro_same-mouse-again-and-again.png){#fig-multilevel-intro-hook fig-align="center" width="85%" fig-alt="Watercolor sketch of one small white mouse hanging from a wire, drawn three times in a row like frames of a film strip, with a wooden tally stick of three notches beside it."}

## Rows are not evidence {#sec-multilevel-intro}

Think of the hanging wire test again: a mouse is put on a wire and has to reach a platform, three attempts a day for three days, and we record how long each crossing took. Suppose a colleague asks how many pieces of evidence you have about how fast the Klf4-KO and the control mice are. You count rows, because that is what the spreadsheet offers, and answer "about 516". Your colleague, who has run this test, raises an eyebrow: those are 63 mice. A mouse that is quick on its first attempt is probably quick on its eighth, for reasons that have nothing to do with genotype: it is lighter, or braver, or has better grip. Its eight crossings are eight looks at the same animal.

@fig-multilevel_clusters shows it for twelve mice, picked to cover the whole range from the fastest to the slowest (every sixth mouse in the order of their own averages, among the mice with all nine attempts). Each row of dots is one mouse, each dot one completed attempt, the black tick is that mouse's own average, and the dashed line is the average of every attempt of every mouse.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Each mouse's own average (log scale) and its number of completed attempts
mouse_mean <- tapply(wire_long$log_wire, wire_long$mouse, mean)
mouse_n <- tapply(wire_long$log_wire, wire_long$mouse, length)

# Twelve mice with all nine attempts, spread evenly over the ordered averages
full_mice <- names(sort(mouse_mean[mouse_n == 9]))
pick <- full_mice[round(seq(1, length(full_mice), length.out = 12))]

# Points and ticks for the picked mice, mouse order set by each one's average
pts <- wire_long[wire_long$mouse %in% pick, ]
pts$mouse <- factor(pts$mouse, levels = pick)
ticks <- data.frame(mouse = factor(pick, levels = pick), m = mouse_mean[pick],
                    pos = seq_along(pick))
grand_mean <- mean(wire_long$log_wire)

# One strip per mouse; dashed line = everyone pooled, tick = this mouse alone
ggplot(pts, aes(y = mouse, x = wire)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = exp(grand_mean), linetype = "dashed", color = "grey35") +
  geom_point(color = "grey50", alpha = 0.8, size = 2) +
  geom_segment(data = ticks, aes(x = exp(m), xend = exp(m), y = pos - 0.32, yend = pos + 0.32),
               linewidth = 1.2) +
  annotate("text", x = exp(grand_mean) * 1.04, y = 12.75, hjust = 0, size = 4.5,
           label = "all mice pooled") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_discrete(expand = expansion(add = c(0.6, 0.9))) +
  labs(x = "Crossing time (s, log scale)", y = "Mouse (fastest at the bottom)") +
  Plot_theme +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), axis.ticks.y = element_blank()) +
  legend_none()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Completed crossing times (log scale) of twelve mice in the hanging wire test. Each row is one mouse and each dot one attempt; the black tick is the mouse's own average and the dashed line is the average of all attempts of all mice.](multilevel-intro_files/figure-html/fig-multilevel_clusters-1.png){#fig-multilevel_clusters fig-alt='Twelve horizontal strips, one per mouse, ordered from the fastest mouse at the bottom to the slowest at the top. Each strip holds up to nine grey dots and one black tick at the mouse\'s own average. A dashed vertical line marks the overall average. The ticks drift from left to right going up the figure, and the dots of each mouse huddle around its own tick, mostly on one side of the dashed line.' width=624}
:::
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Between-mouse and within-mouse variance of the log crossing time
m_icc <- glmmTMB(log_wire ~ 1 + (1 | mouse), data = wire_long)
var_mouse <- as.numeric(VarCorr(m_icc)$cond$mouse[1, 1])
sd_mouse <- sqrt(var_mouse)
sd_resid <- sigma(m_icc)
grand_mu <- fixef(m_icc)$cond[["(Intercept)"]]

# Share of the variance that lies between mice, and the design effect
icc_wire <- var_mouse / (var_mouse + sd_resid^2)
n_mice <- length(unique(wire_long$mouse))
rows_per_mouse <- nrow(wire_long) / n_mice
design_effect <- 1 + (rows_per_mouse - 1) * icc_wire
n_eff <- nrow(wire_long) / design_effect
```
:::






Showing twelve mice instead of all sixty-three is a deliberate choice. The earlier version (@fig-assumptions_independence) had one column per mouse and showed that the whole sample is clustered; here I want you to read single mice, so each gets a row you can follow. A bar plot of means with asterisks would have erased exactly this picture: it would show one number per genotype and hide that the dots of a mouse belong together.

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read this figure"}
Read it in three steps. First, pick one row and look at how far its dots spread. Second, compare that spread with the distance between that mouse's tick and the dashed line. If the dots of every mouse huddled around the dashed line, the rows would be draws from one common distribution and mouse identity would not matter. Third, look at the ticks as a column: they drift from left to right, so some mice really are faster than others. Here the within-mouse spread is clearly smaller than the spread between mice, and that is the whole problem in one picture. A conclusion looks like "attempts of the same mouse resemble each other", with a number attached, which comes next.
:::

The number is the [intraclass correlation]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}, the share of the variance of the log crossing time that lies between mice instead of within them. Its picture is the figure you just read: the more the ticks scatter relative to the dots around each tick, the higher it is. It is 0.35 for these data (a standard deviation between mice of 0.31 and one within mice of 0.42 on the log scale). From it comes the second number, the [design effect]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"} (Kish's formula), which asks how many times too optimistic your sample size is. The idea that clustered rows add up to far fewer independent units of information, and that the model should reflect it, is what Inchausti and Gelman and Vehtari call pseudoreplication [@inchausti2023; @gelman2024]. With $m$ attempts per mouse and intraclass correlation $\rho$, the variance of an average is inflated by a factor of $1 + (m-1)\rho$. Imagine eight copies of the same photograph (@fig-multilevel-intro-copies): they weigh as much as eight photographs, but they show you one scene. Here, 516 rows with about 8.2 per mouse inflate the variance by 3.5, so those rows carry about as much information about a mouse-level quantity as 147 independent ones. A model that counts all 516 as independent evidence will report intervals that are too narrow, and it will do so with a straight face.

![Eight copies of one photograph weigh as much as eight photographs, but they show one scene. That is what a design effect counts.](images/multilevel-intro_eight-copies-one-photograph.png){#fig-multilevel-intro-copies fig-align="center" width="90%" fig-alt="Watercolor sketch of a wooden table with a fan of identical prints of a white mouse hanging from a wire on the left, and on the right four different prints: the same mouse on a wire, a pair of stained brain sections, a single neuron and a spiral of cells, with a dashed arrow from the fan to the different prints."}

::: {.callout-note title="How to report it"}
**Results.** The completed crossing times of the hanging wire test were strongly clustered by mouse: the intraclass correlation of the log crossing time was 0.35, corresponding to a design effect of 3.5 with 8.2 completed attempts per mouse on average. The 516 attempts of 63 mice therefore carry the information of roughly 147 independent observations.

**Methods.** We estimated the intraclass correlation from a Gaussian random-intercept model of the log crossing time with a random intercept per mouse (`glmmTMB`, maximum likelihood), as the between-mouse variance divided by the sum of the between-mouse and residual variances. The design effect was computed as $1 + (m-1)\rho$ with $m$ the mean number of completed attempts per mouse.
:::

## Three ways to estimate how good each mouse is

Having seen that mice differ, the natural next question is the one a lab actually asks: how fast *is* each mouse? There are three honest answers, and the model we are heading for is the third.

Suppose you must estimate the typical crossing time of one particular mouse, and some mice were tested nine times while one was tested only twice. The first answer ignores mice altogether: everyone gets the grand average. This is [complete pooling]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}, the model of the previous two parts (it amounts to assuming that the spread between mice is zero), and it says the mouse's identity carries no information. It is stable and it is wrong for the quick and slow mice alike. The second answer trusts each mouse's own tally and nothing else: the average of its own attempts, fitted separately mouse by mouse. This is [no pooling]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}. It respects individuality, but think about the mouse tested twice. Two attempts can be both fast by luck, and the estimate will believe them completely.

The third answer is the one a sensible colleague would give. Picture a new lab member who has run two sessions on a mouse and finds it astonishingly quick. You would say: "Interesting, but two sessions is two sessions; most mice are around the middle, so I'd bet it is quick but not that quick." You would say something different about a mouse with nine fast attempts: "That one really is fast." Your guess for each mouse is a compromise between what its own attempts say and what mice in general look like, and the compromise leans on the mouse's own data more as there is more of it. That is [partial pooling]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}, and the rubber band of @fig-multilevel-intro-band is the picture I keep in my head: each mouse's own tally is pulled gently toward the group's, and a short tally is pulled harder than a long one.

![Each mouse's own tally is pulled toward the group's by a rubber band. A short tally is pulled harder than a long one.](images/multilevel-intro_rubber-band-to-the-group.png){#fig-multilevel-intro-band fig-align="center" width="85%" fig-alt="Watercolor sketch of a wooden board with a horizontal rail across its middle and eight teal and ochre pegs, some above it and some below, each tied to the rail by a thin rubber band. Dotted circles mark where each peg stood before being pulled, and a small tally stick with few or many notches lies under each peg."}

We can compute all three for the wire data without fitting any heavy model. The no-pooling estimate of a mouse is the average of its own log crossing times, $\bar y_j$. The complete-pooling estimate is the grand average, $\mu$. The partial-pooling estimate falls between them, and its position has a closed form that is worth seeing once, because it holds in every multilevel model of the part (@eq-multilevel-intro-shrink):

$$
\hat\alpha_j = \mu + B_j\,(\bar y_j - \mu), \qquad B_j = \frac{\tau^2}{\tau^2 + \sigma^2 / n_j}
$$ {#eq-multilevel-intro-shrink}

Here $n_j$ is the number of attempts of mouse $j$, $\sigma$ the spread of attempts within a mouse and $\tau$ the spread between mice. $B_j$ is a number between 0 and 1, the weight the mouse's own average gets. Read it as a ratio of two kinds of noise: when the spread between mice ($\tau^2$) is large compared with the noise of a mouse's own average ($\sigma^2/n_j$), the mouse's tally is believable and $B_j$ is near 1; with few attempts or a small spread between mice, $B_j$ falls and the estimate leans on the group. Everything on the right-hand side is estimated from the data by a random-intercept model, which I fit here with `glmmTMB` only because it takes a fraction of a second; the same model in `brms` is the business of @sec-multilevel-varying-intercepts. The check at the end of the next chunk confirms that the closed form and the model's own estimates for each mouse are the same numbers.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Raw average and number of attempts per mouse (the no-pooling estimates)
mice <- data.frame(mouse = names(mouse_n),
                   n = as.numeric(mouse_n),
                   raw = as.numeric(mouse_mean[names(mouse_n)]))

# Weight on the mouse's own average, then the partially pooled estimate
mice$B <- var_mouse / (var_mouse + sd_resid^2 / mice$n)
mice$pooled <- grand_mu + mice$B * (mice$raw - grand_mu)

# Check against the conditional modes the model reports for each mouse
cond_mode <- ranef(m_icc)$cond$mouse[mice$mouse, 1] + grand_mu
check_diff <- max(abs(mice$pooled - cond_mode))

# The mouse with the fewest attempts, and the mice with fewer than nine
few <- mice[which.min(mice$n), ]
n_short <- sum(mice$n < 9)
```
:::






@fig-multilevel_shrinkage shows what that does to all 63 mice (the two estimates agree with the model's own to 4e-16, so this really is what a multilevel model computes). Open circles are the no-pooling averages, filled circles the partially pooled ones, and each arrow runs from one to the other.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Order mice by their own average and flag those with fewer than nine attempts
mice <- mice[order(mice$raw), ]
mice$rank <- seq_len(nrow(mice))
mice$attempts <- ifelse(mice$n < 9, "Fewer than 9 attempts", "All 9 attempts")

# Arrows from the raw average (open) to the shrunken one (filled), in seconds
ggplot(mice, aes(x = rank, color = attempts)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = exp(grand_mu), linetype = "dashed", color = "grey35") +
  geom_segment(aes(y = exp(raw), yend = exp(pooled)),
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.12, "cm"), type = "closed"),
               linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(aes(y = exp(raw)), shape = 1, size = 2) +
  geom_point(aes(y = exp(pooled)), shape = 16, size = 1.6) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("All 9 attempts" = "grey45",
                                "Fewer than 9 attempts" = "#D55E00")) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "Mice (ordered by their own average)",
       y = "Crossing time (s, log scale)", color = NULL) +
  Plot_theme +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), axis.ticks.x = element_blank()) +
  legend_top()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Average crossing time of each mouse without pooling (open circles) and with partial pooling (filled circles). Arrows point toward the overall average (dashed line). Orange arrows mark mice with fewer than nine completed attempts, which are pulled the furthest.](multilevel-intro_files/figure-html/fig-multilevel_shrinkage-1.png){#fig-multilevel_shrinkage fig-alt='Sixty-three mice along the horizontal axis ordered by their own average crossing time, with a dashed horizontal line at the overall average. Each mouse has an open circle at its own average and a filled circle closer to the dashed line, joined by an arrow. Most arrows are short and grey. A handful of orange arrows, for mice with fewer than nine attempts, are noticeably longer, and some of the most extreme open circles sit far from the line.' width=768}
:::
:::






I drew arrows and not two bare sets of points because the pulling *is* the result: a reader should see each estimate move. Package and function are plain `ggplot2` (`geom_segment()` with an arrow head), and the design tip to take home is to draw a before and an after as one connected mark, with the reference value (the dashed line) in the picture, so nobody has to subtract two columns by eye.

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read this figure"}
Start with the dashed line, the overall average. Then pick an open circle far above or below it and follow its arrow: the filled circle at the tip is the estimate that partial pooling would report. The questions to ask, in order, are these. Do the arrows all point toward the dashed line? (They must, that is what pooling does.) Are the long arrows concentrated at the two ends, where the open circles are most extreme? (They are: extreme raw averages are partly luck, and luck gets pulled back.) And which arrows are longest relative to their distance from the line? Look at the orange ones, the mice with fewer attempts. The one mistake to avoid is reading the filled circles as "corrected data". They are estimates of each mouse's typical speed, not measurements.
:::

Three things happen in @fig-multilevel_shrinkage, and each deserves a sentence. Every estimate moves toward the overall average: the most extreme mice move the most in absolute terms, and they move toward the middle, never past it. Most arrows are short, because 46 of the 63 mice have nine attempts and for them $B_j$ is 0.83, which means the model trusts a mouse with nine attempts about 83% and the group about 17%. And mice with fewer attempts move more: the mouse with only 2 attempts has a weight of 0.52, so its own average of 24 seconds is pulled to 21.3, while the overall average is 18.7.

### Shrinkage is not a bias to apologize for

The word [shrinkage]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"} sounds like a loss, as if the model were doing something to your data that you will have to defend. It is the opposite. Think of the first week of a baseball season: the player batting .500 after ten at-bats is not going to finish the season at .500, and nobody who has watched baseball is surprised when the average comes down. The extreme average was partly skill and partly a lucky week, and the lucky part will not repeat. Partial pooling is the arithmetic of that intuition. It does give each mouse's estimate a small pull toward the group, but it does so in exchange for a larger reduction in how wrong the estimates are on average across mice, so the estimates become more useful, not less. McElreath makes the same point with the survival of tadpoles in 48 tanks: partially pooled estimates are better on average because they negotiate between underfitting and overfitting, a regularization whose strength is learned from the data [@mcelreath2020]. Inchausti shows it with schools, where those with few pupils "borrow strength" from the rest [@inchausti2023].

We can check that claim with the wire data themselves and no theory at all (@tbl-multilevel_predict). I held out one completed attempt of every mouse (its last row in the file), fitted the random-intercept model to everything else, and asked how well each kind of estimate predicts the held-out attempt, in squared error on the log scale. This is one split on one dataset, so read it as an illustration and not as a proof.






::: {#tbl-multilevel_predict .cell tbl-cap='Mean squared error, on the log-seconds scale, of three estimates of each mouse\'s typical crossing time when predicting one held-out attempt per mouse. Lower is better.'}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Hold out the last completed attempt of every mouse; train on the rest
last_row <- tapply(wire_long$row, wire_long$mouse, max)
test <- wire_long[wire_long$row %in% last_row, ]
train <- wire_long[!wire_long$row %in% last_row, ]

# Refit the random-intercept model on the training attempts only
m_tr <- glmmTMB(log_wire ~ 1 + (1 | mouse), data = train)
tau2 <- as.numeric(VarCorr(m_tr)$cond$mouse[1, 1])
mu_tr <- fixef(m_tr)$cond[["(Intercept)"]]

# The three estimates per mouse, from training attempts alone
n_tr <- tapply(train$log_wire, train$mouse, length)
raw_tr <- tapply(train$log_wire, train$mouse, mean)
B_tr <- tau2 / (tau2 + sigma(m_tr)^2 / n_tr)
pooled_tr <- mu_tr + B_tr * (raw_tr - mu_tr)

# Compare each with the held-out attempt of the same mouse
y_test <- test$log_wire[match(names(n_tr), test$mouse)]
mse <- c(`Complete pooling (grand average)` = mean((y_test - mu_tr)^2),
         `No pooling (own average)` = mean((y_test - raw_tr)^2),
         `Partial pooling` = mean((y_test - pooled_tr)^2))
knitr::kable(data.frame(Estimate = names(mse), `Mean squared error` = round(mse, 3),
                        check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|Estimate                         | Mean squared error|
|:--------------------------------|------------------:|
|Complete pooling (grand average) |              0.291|
|No pooling (own average)         |              0.198|
|Partial pooling                  |              0.197|


:::
:::






In @tbl-multilevel_predict, complete pooling is clearly the worst, as the clusters of @fig-multilevel_clusters would lead you to expect: it throws away real differences between mice. The gain of partial pooling over no pooling is small here, and that is a finding in itself: with 8 training attempts for most mice, each mouse's own average is already fairly reliable. The advantage grows as the number of attempts per group shrinks, which is the situation of cells per section, sessions per patient, or any design where some groups are thin. @fig-multilevel_pull shows why, and it shows one more thing: the model does not have to be told how much to pool.

## What a multilevel model adds

In @eq-multilevel-intro-shrink the quantity $\tau$, the spread of the mice around the group average, was a number I took from a fitted model. That is the whole idea of a multilevel model, and it is worth stating in words before any notation. A [multilevel model]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"} treats the group-level quantities (each mouse's own typical speed) as draws from a distribution whose spread is itself a parameter, learned from the data together with everything else. The model therefore decides how much to pool: if the mice turn out to be very different from each other, $\tau$ is large and pooling is weak; if they turn out nearly alike, $\tau$ is small and each mouse is pulled hard toward the group. Complete pooling and no pooling are the two ends of this dial, $\tau = 0$ and $\tau = \infty$, and the data choose where on the dial to sit.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Weight on the mouse's own average for 1 to 12 attempts, three group spreads
n_seq <- 1:12
tau_set <- c("Half" = 0.5, "Estimated" = 1, "Twice" = 2) * sd_mouse
pull_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(tau_set), function(lab) {
  tau_k <- tau_set[[lab]]
  data.frame(n = n_seq, spread = lab,
             B = tau_k^2 / (tau_k^2 + sd_resid^2 / n_seq))
}))
pull_df$spread <- factor(pull_df$spread, levels = names(tau_set))

# One curve per spread, with a dot at n = 9 and the legend in the empty lower right
ggplot(pull_df, aes(x = n, y = B, linetype = spread, color = spread)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = pull_df[pull_df$n == 9, ], size = 2.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("grey45", "#0072B2", "#D55E00")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1, 3, 6, 9, 12)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Attempts per mouse", y = "Weight on own average (B)",
       color = "Spread", linetype = "Spread") +
  Plot_theme +
  legend_inside(0.72, 0.25)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Weight a mouse's own average receives (B in the text) as a function of its number of attempts, for the between-mouse spread estimated from the wire data and for half and twice that spread. Dots mark the nine attempts most mice have.](multilevel-intro_files/figure-html/fig-multilevel_pull-1.png){#fig-multilevel_pull fig-alt='Three rising curves of the weight on a mouse\'s own average against the number of attempts from one to twelve. The curve for twice the estimated spread is highest and rises quickest, the one for the estimated spread is in the middle and the one for half the spread is lowest. A dot on each curve marks nine attempts.' width=624}
:::
:::






@fig-multilevel_pull is built from the two spreads this dataset gave us and nothing else (no new data are simulated: the curves are @eq-multilevel-intro-shrink evaluated at different values). Read it from left to right: with one attempt the weight on a mouse's own average is low, and it climbs with every additional attempt; the three curves differ by how different the mice are. For the estimated spread, nine attempts earn a weight of 0.83, the dot on the middle curve. The model's decision about $\tau$ shows up as the position of the curve, and that is why partial pooling is neither a fudge nor a free parameter you must tune by hand.

Now the notation, which I introduced as late as I could. For attempt $i$ of mouse $j$ (here the log crossing time $y_{ij}$), the multilevel model has two lines (@eq-multilevel-intro-model):

$$
y_{ij} \sim \text{Normal}(\alpha_j, \sigma), \qquad \alpha_j \sim \text{Normal}(\mu, \tau)
$$ {#eq-multilevel-intro-model}

The first line is the model you already know, with one difference: each mouse has its own intercept $\alpha_j$. The second line is the new one: those intercepts are themselves drawn from a distribution centered on the group average $\mu$, with spread $\tau$. In the formula syntax of `lme4`, `glmmTMB` and `brms` this is written as an extra term in parentheses, and the whole part runs on two such terms (@tbl-multilevel_vocab).

## The vocabulary of the part

The terms below are used in every chapter ahead. Each has a picture from the wire data, a plain definition and its place in the formula.

+------------------------------------------------------------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------+
| Term                                                             | A picture from the wire data                                                                                                                   | In the formula                                  |
+==================================================================+================================================================================================================================================+=================================================+
| [Level]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}                  | Attempts sit inside mice: attempts are the lower level, mice the upper one. Neurons sit inside patients, cells inside sections inside animals. | the nesting itself, not a term                  |
+------------------------------------------------------------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------+
| [Grouping factor]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}        | The column that says which mouse a row belongs to; its categories are the groups.                                                              | `mouse` in `(1 | mouse)`                        |
+------------------------------------------------------------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------+
| [Varying intercept]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}      | Each mouse has its own baseline speed, drawn from the group of all mice.                                                                       | `(1 | mouse)`                                   |
+------------------------------------------------------------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------+
| [Varying slope]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}          | Each mouse also has its own rate of improving from one day to the next.                                                                        | `(1 + day | mouse)`                             |
+------------------------------------------------------------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------+
| [Intraclass correlation]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"} | The share of variance that lies between mice, about 0.35 for the wire crossing times.                                        | $\tau^2 / (\tau^2 + \sigma^2)$                  |
+------------------------------------------------------------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------+
| [Design effect]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}          | How many times the variance of an average is inflated by the clustering, 3.5 here.                                     | $1 + (m-1)\rho$                                 |
+------------------------------------------------------------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------+
| [Shrinkage]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}              | The pull of each group's estimate toward the overall average, harder for thin groups.                                                          | the weight $B_j$ in @eq-multilevel-intro-shrink |
+------------------------------------------------------------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------+

: The vocabulary of the multilevel part, each term with its picture and its place in the model formula. {#tbl-multilevel_vocab}

Read @tbl-multilevel_vocab down the third column. `(1 | mouse)` says "give every mouse its own intercept, drawn from a common distribution", which is the model of @eq-multilevel-intro-model. `(1 + day | mouse)` says "give every mouse its own intercept *and* its own slope over days, and let the two be correlated, so that fast mice may also improve more or less than slow ones". The bar `|` reads as "within": a varying term for the things on its left, within each level of the grouping factor on its right. These terms are added to the usual formula, so a model with a genotype effect looks like `log_wire ~ genotype + (1 | mouse)`: the genotype is the part you already know, the parenthesis is the new part.

A word on names, because you will meet several vocabularies in the literature. Older books speak of "fixed" and "random" effects, and the words mean different things in different books. Gelman, Hill and Vehtari avoid "fixed-effects model" because it is used in ambiguous ways in the statistics literature [@gelman2020], and Gelman's own survey of the textbooks finds several definitions of fixed and random effects that contradict each other [@gelman2005]. McElreath calls this a swamp of vocabulary and adopts Gelman's terms [@mcelreath2020]. Inchausti adds a case every bench scientist will recognize: if "random" means that the levels were sampled at random from a larger population, then the five treatments you chose on purpose, or the 26 countries of the European Union, can never be random effects, although the model for them is exactly the same [@inchausti2023]. Following these authors, in this book I say [varying]{.ix} intercepts and slopes for the quantities that differ between groups and are modeled as draws from a distribution, and [group-level]{.ix ix="group-level effect"} for that distribution's parameters ($\mu$, $\tau$). The single numbers that apply to everyone (a genotype coefficient) are population-level coefficients, which is also how `brms` prints them. The names say what the model does, which "fixed" and "random" do not: a varying intercept is a parameter with a probability distribution of its own, and in the Bayesian reading that distribution is a prior whose amount of regularization is learned from the data.

## What this part does with it

Eight chapters follow, in an order that goes from the simplest use of the idea to the cases where it meets a different problem. I will say honestly, for each, which loose thread of the last two parts it ties.

**First we untangle cells, sections and animals** (@sec-multilevel-varying-intercepts). This is the chapter the whole book has been promising: pseudoreplication in cellular neuroscience, with the histology data going below the animal level, where the independence of rows stops being true. It closes the thread of @sec-linear-regression-assumptions, with the varying intercept as the repair.

**Then each animal gets its own response** (@sec-multilevel-varying-slopes). The same data, extended: animals differ not only in where they start but in how they respond, and the varying slope with its correlation is the tool for that.

**Next the families come back** (@sec-multilevel-glmm). Trials inside neurons inside patients, and the wire trials: the random intercept per neuron previewed in @sec-count-regression and the trial-level overdispersion of @sec-beta-robust-regression become proper models, and the question of whether the zeros and the overdispersion were really neurons and mice differing from each other gets its answer.

**We then grade neurological deficit** (@sec-ordinal-nominal-regression). This one is not about independence. It fills the last row of @tbl-glm_families, the ordered categories, with the neurological score of mice after ischemia and with the graded items of a neurologist's examination, and then goes on to categories that have no order at all.

**After that we model two markers and their spread together** (@sec-multivariate-distributional-regression). The variance problem that @sec-linear-regression-assumptions and @sec-linear-regression-multiple left open and that [the introduction to GLMs](glm-intro.qmd#sec-glm-intro) pointed here, a single $\sigma$ that is too stingy for one day and too generous for another, becomes a model of $\sigma$ itself, and GFAP and PDGFR-β are modeled jointly.

**Then we follow the scar over thirty days** (@sec-longitudinal-timeseries). The full time course of the histology data and the open-field animals measured on six days: the dependence between the days of the same animal, which can be a trait of the animal or a memory of the previous session, and which the chapter checks before modeling; the independence discussion named it and set it aside.

**Next we deal with values the microscope cannot see** (@sec-missing-data-measurement-error). Missing data, measurement error and censoring pick up the thread of @sec-eda-missing-data: imputation recast as parameter estimation, and limits of detection as part of the model.

**And we close by asking what causes what, and drawing curves** (@sec-causal-inference-splines). Causal diagrams for the adjustment questions that @sec-linear-regression-multiple and @sec-linear-models-reflection raised, and splines as a flexible way to hold a variable fixed and to ask whether a relationship bends. (The curved time course where a straight line failed in the first part got its own answer in @sec-longitudinal-timeseries, because five distinct days are too few for a spline.)

Part 6 follows, on spatial and structural analysis ([Reading the geometry of tissue](spatial-intro.qmd)). I mention it here because spatial dependence is the same independence problem in another dress: cells that sit close together resemble each other in the way attempts of one mouse do, and the tools of this part are what make it tractable.

## Three things to know before you start

First, **multilevel models need enough groups, not only enough rows**. A thousand trials from three patients tell you a great deal about those three patients and rather little about the spread of patients in general, because $\tau$ is estimated from the *groups*, and three groups are three data points for it. Inchausti puts numbers on it, with the caveat that the question is unresolved: with very few levels the variance of the varying effect is biased and imprecise, and the rule of thumb he reports for linear models is at least five levels with more than ten replicates each, while for binary and count outcomes fewer than about fifteen clusters with fewer than ten rows each risks non-convergence and badly biased variances [@inchausti2023]. With two or three groups there is almost nothing to pool, and Kruschke shows that with few groups and a broad prior the hierarchical structure can do little good or can shrink the groups too hard [@kruschke2015]. In a frequentist fit the usual symptom is an estimate of $\tau$ that collapses to exactly zero; in a Bayesian fit it is a very wide posterior for $\tau$, whose uncertainty flows into every group's estimate. We will meet this with the neurons of @sec-multilevel-glmm.

Second, **the group-level standard deviation needs a prior**, and a weakly informative one is the book's default: an exponential distribution on $\tau$. The old habit of an inverse-gamma with tiny parameters distorts the estimate near zero, and Gelman showed that half-normal, half-Student-*t* and similar distributions behave better [@gelman2006; @gelman2026]. Exponential, half-normal and half-Student-*t* priors all leave finite density at zero, so the data can shrink $\tau$ to nothing if the groups do not differ, and they decay to the right, so absurdly large spreads are ruled out. They do not keep the estimate away from zero, and Kruschke warns that with small datasets even such priors can produce implosive shrinkage, in which case a prior with a nonzero mode, one that says that no variation between groups is implausible, may express what you know better [@kruschke2015]. How to choose and check priors is the subject of @sec-priors-regularization, and the same prior predictive thinking applies.

Third, **these models are slower and their warnings are louder**. Every varying intercept is a parameter, so a model with sixty-three mice has sixty-three more than the one without, and the sampler can struggle when $\tau$ is close to zero (divergent transitions, treedepth warnings). Those warnings, and what to do about them, are explained in @sec-mcmc-model-checking; read that chapter's section on divergences before the first multilevel fit.

The frequentist counterpart stays alongside, as everywhere in the book. The same formulas, `(1 | mouse)` and `(1 + day | mouse)`, are written for `lme4` (`lmer()`, `glmer()`) and `glmmTMB`, and the partial pooling mechanism is the same one. The most characteristic failure of the frequentist fit is the *singular fit*: the estimated spread between groups collapses to exactly zero (or the correlation between a varying intercept and slope to plus or minus one), the software warns that the fit is on a boundary, and what you have learned is that the data cannot tell the groups apart, not that the groups are identical. A weakly informative prior on $\tau$ gives the Bayesian fit a whole posterior to work with instead of a single estimate that can land on the boundary.

So let's meet the mice again, this time as mice. On to @sec-multilevel-varying-intercepts.
